segments.text: Hello.
Day thirty.
A little over five weeks ago, I said hi, and told you that you didn't have to quit that day.
You kept using, and you watched.
You found the gap and gave it a name.
You learned to ride a wave.
You wrote yourself a note, and the next morning you held your thumb down and began.
Then you did thirty days.
I only talked.
On the morning of Day Xero, I said that you weren't someone who couldn't use.
You were someone who didn't need to.
Back then, that was something to aim for.
Look at it now.
There's a difference between a person who is trying not to use nicotine, and a person who doesn't.
The first one is holding a door shut.
The second has simply walked on.
They aren't being strong.
There's nothing pulling at them.
Somewhere in the last thirty days, on a day you probably didn't notice, you started becoming the second kind.
That doesn't mean it's over.
Certain places, smells and moments can still set off a craving, even weeks after you stop.
Each time you get through one, that link tends to get weaker.
And you know what to do with a wave.
One last time, let's listen for it.
Take a breath, in a way that feels comfortable for you.
Remember the faucet from your first day.
The drip in another room, and the quiet when it stops.
Go looking for the gap.
Check the places you used to find it.
And notice what's there now.
This quiet isn't a reward for getting through thirty days.
It's just what your days are like now.
Now say it to yourself, once, in your own head.
"I don't use nicotine."
Not "I'm trying to quit."
Not "I've given up."
Just that.
Notice how it sits.
In a moment, your reasons will be on your screen, the ones you wrote before any of this.
Then your thirty days, in numbers.
And in a few moments, you'll hold to graduate.
Take your time with it.
The daily part of the program ends here.
But I'm not going far.
I'll check in a few more times over the coming months, because some old cues take their time coming round.
Craving SOS, your plan and your toolkit stay exactly where they are.
You did this.
One wave at a time.
Thank you for letting me keep you company.
